<Rep. Maxine Waters, Rep. Nydia M. Velázquez, Rep. Al Green, Rep. Brad Sherman, Rep. Emanuel Cleaver, Rep. Bill Foster, Rep. Juan Vargas, Rep. Ayanna Pressley, Rep. Nikema Williams, Rep. Joyce Beatty, Rep. Sean Casten, Rep. Sylvia R. Garcia>: President Trump also released an executive order stating that rules drafted by Federal financial regulators must be reviewed and approved by the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (OIRA) within the White House's Office of Management and Budget (OMB).\22\ Financial agencies like the Federal Reserve (Fed), Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC), Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC), the National Credit Union Association (NCUA), the SEC, and the CFTC have traditionally issued regulations independent of the political influence of the White House. However, when conducting these reviews, OIRA must now run an interagency review process to allow other agencies to provide feedback as well.\23\ As a result, Trump and others in his Administration would also have a direct hand in reviewing and modifying the rules implementing the CALAMITY Act to maximize profits for the crypto companies they own. The CALAMITY Act does nothing to address these massive conflicts of interest, allowing the President and his family, along with others in his Administration, to gain from their government positions, ensuring the new regulatory framework works best for their digital assets, if not outright undermining competing digital asset products. Testifying before the Committee, one panelist, Bartlett Naylor, a Financial Policy Advocate at Public Citizen, urged Congress to ``not abdicate any powers to hold Trump accountable. Without conflict-of-interest guardrails, approving these bills effectively endorses Trump's conflicts. The bills will integrate crypto into mainstream banking, serving to fatten his grift.''\24\
\22\Federal Register, Executive Order 14215--Ensuring Accountability for All Agencies (Feb. 18, 2025).
\23\See Obama White House Archives, About OIRA (accessed Apr. 10, 2025).
\24\House Committee on Financial Services, Testimony of Bartlett Collins Naylor, Democratic Minority Day: Continuation of American Innovation and the Future of Digital Assets: From Blueprint to a Functional Framework, 119th Cong. (June 6, 2025).
INCREASED INVESTOR HARM
The CALAMITY Act includes several sections that will increase and create new harm to investors. A few of these provisions include:
1. Section 106 creates a provisional registration
process that would allow entities to escape regulation
and oversight while the rules of the bill are written.
To make matters worse, the provisional registration
process is silent on whether the SEC or state
regulators may bring enforcement actions against an
entity that has filed a statement of provisional
registration, so harmed investors would have little
recourse from these entities.
2. Section 202 would bring unprecedented risk to
investors through a new exemption at the SEC, labeled
the 4(a)(8) exemption. It would allow crypto firms to
raise $75 million per year for four years, if they
intend to become a ``mature blockchain system'' (which
is explained below). This exemption allows firms to
engage in general solicitation of retail investors,
which means that everyday investors could be peddled
securities, which would not include audited financials
or issuer obligations to continually disclose material
facts about the project. Non-accredited investors
(i.e., retail investors) would be able to purchase
crypto assets up to all of their net worth or annual
income, which is a stark contrast to the Regulation A
(``Reg A'') exemption, which limits non-accredited
investors to investing up to 10% of their income or net
worth.\25\ Firms taking advantage of Reg A must provide
audited financials,\26\ a business description,
material risk factors, use of proceeds, and other
disclosures.\27\ They also are subject to ongoing
reporting requirements\28\ and SEC approval\29\ for the
offering.\30\ Most worryingly, state securities
regulators are explicitly barred from regulating this
new exempt offering even though the SEC rarely brings
enforcement actions when harms are small. And
inexplicably, there are no requirements that the funds
raised by a crypto company must go towards developing
the crypto business or its blockchain, as is required
of other securities offerings.
\25\17 CFR Sec. 230.251(d)(2)(C).
\26\17 CFR Sec. 230.252(d) (``An offering statement must contain audited financial statements for Tier 2 offerings.'').
\27\17 CFR Sec. 239.90--Form 1-A content requirements.
\28\17 CFR Sec. 230.257--Ongoing reporting obligations for Tier 2 issuers.
\29\SEC approval is also referred to as the term, ``qualification.''
\30\17 CFR Sec. 230.251(d)(2)(i) (``No sale of securities may be made until the offering statement has been qualified by order of the Commission.'').
3. Section 205 creates a mechanism for ``digital
commodity issuer, digital commodity related person,
digital commodity affiliated person, or decentralized
governance system of the blockchain system'' to escape
SEC oversight by self-certifying that their blockchain
is a ``mature blockchain.'' Section 205 defines a
``mature blockchain system'' as--among other criteria
related to its functions--a blockchain that ``is not
controlled by any person or group of persons under
common control.''\31\ However, this threshold raises
various issues. According to testimony from Lee
Reiners, a Lecturing Fellow at Duke University, ``There
have been several examples of venture capital firms
controlling less than 20% of governance tokens and
still exerting considerable influence over a digital
asset.''\32\ This section also allows a loophole for
unilateral control to carry out ``regular maintenance''
and ``cyber security.'' Furthermore, there is an
exemption for ``preexisting blockchains''' that existed
before the enactment of the bill, where ``at least 50
percent of the units of the digital commodity related
to the blockchain system are held by persons other than
the digital commodity issuer, a digital commodity
related person, or a digital commodity affiliated
person.'' Once an entity self-certifies to the SEC that
its blockchain is mature, the SEC only has 60 days to
stay this self-certification (there being no proper
oversight mechanisms for the SEC to be able to confirm
that information in the self-certification application
is materially true). If the SEC is unable to institute
a stay, the blockchain is deemed as ``mature'' and any
existing assets issued on that blockchain, or future
assets, would not be subject to SEC's rules. Finally,
SEC's resources are not what they used to be: the Trump
Administration's SEC Budget request for FY2026 is lower
than Biden Administration's enacted FY2024 levels and
the SEC has already suffered an unprecedented level of
exodus of seasoned staff (by some estimates, over 15%
of its workforce has left the Commission)\33\ and so
its engagement with potentially hundreds of entities
rushing to submit their self-certifications would be
impracticable.
\31\Section 205, ANS to H.R. 3633.
\32\House Committee on Financial Services, Testimony of Lee Reiners, Dazed and Confused: Breaking Down the SEC's Politicized Approach to Digital Assets, 118th Cong. (Sept. 18, 2024).
\33\US SEC's new chief says 15% of staff have left, contract cuts to come, sources say, Reuters (May 6, 2025).
4. Section 404 and Section 406 allow customers to
waive segregation requirements, related to how the
entity must hold the assets of multiple customers, for
participating in certain blockchain services. If this
waiver is not clarified, it could be buried in small
print terms and conditions, where investors would waive
their protections without fully understanding how their
assets could be put at risk.
Additionally, there are no criminal penalties for violations of the new prohibitions included in the bill or a private right of action for harmed individuals to recover losses. Without incentives to comply with the bill, innovation in this space may not move towards productive use cases but towards memecoins, rug pulls, and pump and dump schemes.\34\ To make matters worse, under Section 302, the SEC's ability to proactively address investor protection concerns would be limited to responding to fraud after it happens. In fact, the SEC is prohibited from issuing reporting requirements, procedures, or standards to prevent fraud, manipulation, or insider trading.
\34\See, e.g., Lin William Cong, et. al., Crypto Wash Trading, NBER Working Paper Series (Dec. 2022). (``wash trading on each unregulated exchange . . . averaged over 70% of the reported volume''); Molly White, Web3 is Going Just Great (accessed June 1, 2025). Crypto grifts and disasters stand at $78 billion.
NATIONAL SECURITY
The CALAMITY Act endangers our country's national security and ignores Trump's elimination of important defenses against criminal activity facilitated by crypto. Since taking office, Trump has undone Congress' decades-long crime-fighting laws and enforcement rules, effectively removing the resources and examiners that serve our national security but which could also check presidents' self-profiteering.\35\ Trump has fired examiners, Inspector Generals, gutted the Corporate Transparency Act, frozen enforcement of the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act, and disbanded the Department of Justice (DOJ) National Cryptocurrency Enforcement Team.\36\ Further, in line with Trump's executive orders, the SEC and other agencies are rescinding regulations and intentionally failing to carry out critical enforcement actions, including suspending several cases for Trump donors and Trump's crypto investors.\37\
\35\Trump Staffed his Cabinet with wealthy advisers. Some stand to gain even more from recent policy shifts, CNN (Apr. 24, 2025).
\36\Global Financial Integrity, Global Financial Integrity Expresses Deep Concern Over the Suspension of Enforcement of the Corporate Transparency Act (Mar. 13, 2025); National Law Review, 10 Reasons Why FCPA Compliance Is Critically Important for Businesses (July 24, 2020); Law Enforcement, Members of Congress Protest Gutting of Corporate Transparency Act: Just the FACTs, FACT Coalition (Apr. 3, 2025).
\37\White House, Ensuring Lawful Governance and Implementing the President's ``Department Of Government Efficiency'' Deregulatory Initiative (Feb. 19, 2025).
Exacerbating the harm done by this bill and despite repeated warnings to the contrary, the text fails to include authorization for an increase in the CFTC examiners corps. This is despite the considerable number that would be required to adequately enforce the bill's provisions, especially given the projected flood of registrations; Republicans have chosen to send this segment of the crypto industry to an agency that they know cannot sufficiently manage the workload and have refused to provide additional resources to do so. Hilary Allen, a law professor at American University, described the CFTC's resource challenges in her testimony:
The CFTC is widely regarded to be the crypto
industry's preferred regulator. It is a much smaller
agency with a much smaller budget than the SEC, and
unlike the SEC, it has no statutory investor protection
mandate and limited experience regulating retail-
dominated markets.\38\
\38\House Committee on Financial Services, Testimony of Hilary J. Allen, Democratic Minority Day: Continuation of American Innovation and the Future of Digital Assets: From Blueprint to a Functional Framework , 119th Cong. (June 6, 2025).
The bill is also devoid of any meaningful national security provisions. Timothy Massad, emphasized this during his testimony, stating, ``it is surprising to me how little is said about the risks of illicit finance in the Clarity Act.''\39\ And separately, Carole House, Senior Fellow, Atlantic Council, GeoEconomics Center echoed these concerns at the Democratic Minority Day Hearing, highlighting that:
\39\House Committee on Financial Services, Testimony of Timothy G. Massad, Democratic Minority Day: Continuation of American Innovation and the Future of Digital Assets: From Blueprint to a Functional Framework, 119th Cong. (June 6, 2025).
